intro: These patterns sit on a verb and say how the action stands in time: as a life experience, as something in progress or a state left behind, as finished for good, done in advance, tried out, moving towards or away from now, or caught at one exact phase. Most are te-form + a helper verb whose own meaning still shows through: いる 'be there', しまう 'put away', おく 'put down', みる 'look', くる / いく 'come / go'. Pick the helper by asking what that literal verb would add to the picture.

skills.rule: Past plain form + ことがある: 'I have (at some point) done it'; ことがない: 'I have never done it'.
skills.explain:
〜たことがある reports an experience you own: 富士山に登ったことがある 'I have climbed Mount Fuji (at some time in my life)'. It answers 'Have you ever ...?', so the event is undated and usually not routine. Questions are 〜たことがありますか, the negative is 〜たことがない, and 一度も ... たことがない means 'never once'.

Two limits. It does not attach to a pinpointed time: 'I saw a film yesterday' is 昨日映画を見ました, plain past. And it sounds odd for things everyone does every day (朝ご飯を食べたことがある) unless the experience is notable.

Watch the form before こと. Past た + ことがある = experience. Dictionary form + ことがある = 'it sometimes happens': 電車が遅れることがある 'the train is sometimes late'.
patterns: [verb た-form] ことがある / ありますか
[verb た-form] ことがない / ありません
一度も [verb た-form] ことがない

examples.jp: 寿司[すし]を食[た]べ{たことがあります}。
examples.en: I have eaten sushi.

examples.jp: 日本[にほん]に行[い]っ{たことがありますか}。
examples.en: Have you ever been to Japan?

examples.jp: 富士山[ふじさん]に登[のぼ]っ{たことがある}。
examples.en: I've climbed Mount Fuji.

examples.jp: 一度[いちど]も飛行機[ひこうき]に乗[の]っ{たことがない}。
examples.en: I've never once been on a plane.

examples.jp: 子供[こども]の頃[ころ]、この川[かわ]で泳[およ]い{だことがあります}。
examples.en: I swam in this river once when I was a child.

contrast.note: Dictionary form + ことがある means 'sometimes happens': 寿司を食べることがある 'I sometimes eat sushi', not 'I have eaten sushi'.
Ability, not experience: 泳ぐことができる 'I can swim'; 泳いだことがある 'I have swum (at some point)'.
A decision: 行くことにした 'I decided to go'. Nothing has happened yet.

mistakes.bad: 昨日[きのう]、映画[えいが]を見[み]{たことがあります}。
mistakes.good: 昨日[きのう]、映画[えいが]を{見[み]ました}。
mistakes.note: A dated single event is plain past; たことがある is for undated life experience.

mistakes.bad: 寿司[すし]を{食[た]べることがあります}。
mistakes.good: 寿司[すし]を{食[た]べたことがあります}。
mistakes.note: Meaning 'I have eaten sushi', the verb must be past た; dictionary form says 'I sometimes eat it'.

skills.tip: Can you add 'ever' to the English and no date? Then た + ことがある.

skills.rule: Te-form + いる: an action in progress, the state a change has left behind, or a habit; which one depends on the verb.
skills.explain:
With action verbs that take time (食べる, 読む, 降る, 走る) 〜ている means 'is doing': 雨が降っている 'it is raining'. With change verbs that happen in an instant (結婚する, 開く, 来る, 死ぬ, 知る) it means the resulting state: 結婚している 'is married', not 'is getting married'; 窓が開いている 'the window is open'; 来ている 'has come and is here'. With a repeated action it is a habit or job: 毎朝走っている, 銀行で働いている.

The classic trap is 知る. 'I know' is 知っている, but 'I don't know' is 知らない / 知りません, never 知っていない. 行っている means 'has gone and is there now', not 'is going'.

In speech the い often drops: 食べてる, 知ってる. A finished event is た: 結婚した 'got married'; the ongoing state is している.
patterns: [action verb て] いる  (is doing)
[change verb て] いる  (is in the resulting state)
[repeated action て] いる  (habit, job)

examples.jp: 今[いま]、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っ{ています}。
examples.en: It's raining now.

examples.jp: 弟[おとうと]は部屋[へや]で寝[ね]{ている}。
examples.en: My little brother is asleep in his room.

examples.jp: 窓[まど]が開[あ]い{ています}よ。
examples.en: The window is open, you know.

examples.jp: 姉[あね]はもう結婚[けっこん]し{ています}。
examples.en: My older sister is already married.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さんの電話番号[でんわばんごう]を知[し]っ{ていますか}。
examples.en: Do you know Mr Tanaka's phone number?

examples.jp: 父[ちち]は毎朝[まいあさ]公園[こうえん]を走[はし]っ{ている}。
examples.en: My father runs in the park every morning.

contrast.note: てある uses a transitive verb with が and says someone set it up on purpose: 窓が開けてある 'the window has been (deliberately) opened'. ている with the intransitive just describes the state: 窓が開いている.
た reports the event: 結婚した 'got married'. ている reports the state now: 結婚している 'is married'.
ておく is doing something in advance for later; ている only describes what is going on or the state now.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]の名前[なまえ]を{知[し]っていません}。
mistakes.good: 先生[せんせい]の名前[なまえ]を{知[し]りません}。
mistakes.note: 'Know' is 知っている, but 'don't know' is plain 知らない / 知りません.

mistakes.bad: 姉[あね]は結婚[けっこん]{します}。
mistakes.good: 姉[あね]は結婚[けっこん]{しています}。
mistakes.note: Meaning 'my sister is married': a state after a change is ている; します means 'will marry'.

mistakes.bad: 窓[まど]が{開[あ]けています}。
mistakes.good: 窓[まど]が{開[あ]いています}。
mistakes.note: With が, the state of the window needs the intransitive 開く; 開けている is someone doing the opening.

skills.tip: Ask: does the verb take time (then 'is doing') or happen in a flash (then 'is in that state')?

skills.rule: Te-form + しまう: the action is completely finished, or it happened and I regret it or did not mean it; casual ちゃう / じゃう.
skills.explain:
しまう literally means 'put away'. 〜てしまう closes the action off, with two shades. Completion: 宿題を全部やってしまった 'I've got all my homework done'. Regret or accident: 傘を忘れてしまった 'I (went and) left my umbrella behind'. Which one is meant comes from context; with mishaps (落とす, 忘れる, 割る, 遅れる) it is almost always regret.

In speech てしまう becomes ちゃう and でしまう becomes じゃう: 食べちゃった, 飲んじゃった. Past ちゃった is very common. Non-past warns about an outcome: 早く寝ないと風邪をひいちゃうよ 'you'll end up catching a cold'.

Plain た states the fact neutrally; adding てしまう tells the listener how you feel about it. Doing something now so it is ready for later is ておく, not てしまう.
patterns: [verb て] しまう / しまった  (done completely; oops)
[verb て→ちゃう / で→じゃう]  (casual)
[verb て] しまいました  (polite)

examples.jp: 電車[でんしゃ]に傘[かさ]を忘[わす]れ{てしまった}。
examples.en: I left my umbrella on the train.

examples.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]はもう全部[ぜんぶ]やっ{てしまいました}。
examples.en: I've already finished all my homework.

examples.jp: 大事[だいじ]なコップを割[わ]っ{てしまいました}。
examples.en: I broke a cup that mattered a lot to me.

examples.jp: ケーキを一人[ひとり]で全部[ぜんぶ]食[た]べ{ちゃった}。
examples.en: I ate the whole cake by myself.

examples.jp: 早[はや]く寝[ね]ないと、風邪[かぜ]をひい{ちゃう}よ。
examples.en: If you don't go to bed early, you'll end up catching a cold.

contrast.note: ておく is deliberate preparation: 予約しておいた 'I booked it in advance'. てしまう is completion or something unwanted.
てみる is trying out; nothing in it says the action went wrong or is finished.
てある describes a state someone set up on purpose (窓が開けてある); てしまう is about the doer finishing or regretting the act.

mistakes.bad: 財布[さいふ]を落[お]と{しておきました}。
mistakes.good: 財布[さいふ]を落[お]と{してしまいました}。
mistakes.note: Dropping a wallet is an accident; ておく would mean you did it on purpose, in advance.

mistakes.bad: ビールを全部[ぜんぶ]飲[の]ん{ちゃった}。
mistakes.good: ビールを全部[ぜんぶ]飲[の]ん{じゃった}。
mistakes.note: When the te-form ends in で, the casual form is じゃう, not ちゃう.

skills.tip: Could you add 'oops' or 'all of it' to the English? てしまう.

skills.rule: Te-form + おく: do something now, on purpose, so it is ready for later (or leave things as they are); casual とく / どく.
skills.explain:
おく literally means 'put down'. 〜ておく is doing an action and leaving its result in place for a future need: 旅行の前にホテルを予約しておく 'book the hotel before the trip (so it's ready)'. It covers preparation (調べておく, 買っておく), leaving something as is (窓を開けておいて 'leave the window open'), and doing something now for convenience (先に払っておく).

The doer acts on purpose, so the verb must be volitional: no 雨が降っておく. Requests are 〜ておいてください, offers or plans 〜ておきます / ておこう.

In speech ておく contracts to とく and でおく to どく: 言っとくけど 'I'm telling you now', 読んどいて 'read it beforehand'.
patterns: [verb て] おく  (in advance, for later)
[verb て] おいてください  (please do it ahead / leave it)
[verb て→とく / で→どく]  (casual)

examples.jp: 旅行[りょこう]の前[まえ]にホテルを予約[よやく]し{ておきます}。
examples.en: I'll book the hotel before the trip.

examples.jp: 飲[の]み物[もの]は冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に入[い]れ{ておいた}よ。
examples.en: I've put the drinks in the fridge (ready for later).

examples.jp: 会議[かいぎ]の資料[しりょう]をコピーし{ておいて}ください。
examples.en: Please copy the meeting documents beforehand.

examples.jp: 寝[ね]る前[まえ]に目覚[めざ]まし時計[どけい]をセットし{ておこう}。
examples.en: I'll set the alarm clock before I go to bed.

examples.jp: 暑[あつ]いから、窓[まど]は開[あ]け{ておいて}。
examples.en: It's hot, so leave the window open.

contrast.note: てしまう is finishing or an unwanted result; ておく is a planned step taken for later.
ておく is the doer's act of preparing (予約しておいた 'I booked it'); てある describes the prepared state, with the object on が (予約がしてある 'it has been booked').
てみる is doing something to see how it turns out; ておく is doing it because you will need it.

mistakes.bad: パーティーの前[まえ]に飲[の]み物[もの]を買[か]っ{てみました}。
mistakes.good: パーティーの前[まえ]に飲[の]み物[もの]を買[か]っ{ておきました}。
mistakes.note: Meaning 'bought drinks in advance': preparation is ておく; てみる is 'tried buying'.

mistakes.bad: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っ{ておきました}。
mistakes.good: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っ{てきました}。
mistakes.note: ておく needs a deliberate doer; rain cannot prepare anything. 'It started to rain' is 降ってきた.

skills.tip: 'Ready for later' or 'leave it like that'? ておく.

skills.rule: Te-form + みる: do something to see what it is like or how it turns out.
skills.explain:
みる means 'look', so 〜てみる is 'do it and see': この服を着てみてもいいですか 'may I try this on?', 新しい店に行ってみた 'I went to the new shop (to see what it was like)'. Common forms: てみたい 'want to try', てみてください 'try it', てみる？ 'want to try?'. It is the polite way to suggest something without pressure: 先生に聞いてみたら？

てみる is not 'try hard to'. An effort that may fail is 〜ようとする: 起きようとしたが起きられなかった. In practice てみる usually means the action did happen, as a test.

As a helper verb みる is written in kana, not 見る.
patterns: [verb て] みる / みた  (try and see)
[verb て] みたい  (want to try)
[verb て] みてください / みたら？  (suggest trying)

examples.jp: 新[あたら]しいラーメン屋[や]に行[い]っ{てみました}。
examples.en: I tried the new ramen shop.

examples.jp: ちょっと食[た]べ{てみる}？
examples.en: Want to try a bite?

examples.jp: 一度[いちど]、着物[きもの]を着[き]{てみたい}です。
examples.en: I'd like to try wearing a kimono once.

examples.jp: 分[わ]からなければ、先生[せんせい]に聞[き]い{てみて}ください。
examples.en: If you don't understand, try asking the teacher.

examples.jp: この靴[くつ]、履[は]い{てみても}いいですか。
examples.en: May I try these shoes on?

contrast.note: Trying with effort, often failing: 起きようとした 'I tried to get up'. てみる is testing something out.
ておく prepares for later; てみる is curiosity about the result.
てしまう finishes or regrets the act; てみる says nothing about regret.

mistakes.bad: 何度[なんど]も起[お]き{てみました}が、起[お]きられませんでした。
mistakes.good: 何度[なんど]も起[お]き{ようとしました}が、起[お]きられませんでした。
mistakes.note: A failed effort is ようとする; てみる means you did it to see.

mistakes.bad: このお菓子[かし]、食[た]べて{見[み]て}ください。
mistakes.good: このお菓子[かし]、食[た]べ{てみて}ください。
mistakes.note: As a helper verb, みる is written in kana.

skills.tip: Can you add 'and see' to the English? てみる.

skills.rule: Te-form + くる moves towards me or towards now; te-form + いく moves away from me or from now on.
skills.explain:
Use the literal meaning first. In space, 〜てくる means 'do and come (back)': 飲み物を買ってくる 'go and buy a drink (and come back)', 鳥が飛んできた 'a bird flew this way'. 〜ていく means 'do and go': 傘を持っていく 'take an umbrella', 飛んでいった 'flew away'. 行ってきます, said on leaving, is this pattern.

In time, くる is change up to now, いく is change from now on: 日本語が分かってきた 'I've come to understand Japanese', これからも続けていく 'I will keep it up from now on', 人口は減っていく 'the population will go on falling'. 〜てくる also marks the onset of something the speaker notices: 雨が降ってきた 'it has started to rain', お腹が空いてきた.

Pick by direction: towards the speaker or present = くる; away from them or into the future = いく.
patterns: [verb て] くる  (do and come back; towards me)
[verb て] いく  (do and go; away from me)
[change verb て] きた / いく  (up to now / from now on)

examples.jp: コンビニで飲[の]み物[もの]を買[か]っ{てきます}。
examples.en: I'll go and get a drink at the convenience store.

examples.jp: 急[きゅう]に雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っ{てきた}。
examples.en: It suddenly started to rain.

examples.jp: 日本語[にほんご]がだんだん分[わ]かっ{てきました}。
examples.en: I've gradually come to understand Japanese.

examples.jp: 鳥[とり]が南[みなみ]へ飛[と]ん{でいった}。
examples.en: The birds flew away to the south.

examples.jp: これからも日本語[にほんご]の勉強[べんきょう]を続[つづ]け{ていきます}。
examples.en: I'll keep on studying Japanese from now on.

examples.jp: この町[まち]の人口[じんこう]はこれから減[へ]っ{ていく}だろう。
examples.en: This town's population will probably keep falling.

contrast.note: 買ってみる is 'try buying'; 買ってくる is 'go and buy (and come back)'.
持っておく is 'keep hold of it for later'; 持っていく is 'take it along'.
てしまう finishes or regrets; it has no direction in space or time.

mistakes.bad: 最近[さいきん]、寒[さむ]くなっ{ていきました}。
mistakes.good: 最近[さいきん]、寒[さむ]くなっ{てきました}。
mistakes.note: A change that has led up to now is てきた; ていく points into the future.

mistakes.bad: 将来[しょうらい]も日本[にほん]に住[す]み続[つづ]け{てきます}。
mistakes.good: 将来[しょうらい]も日本[にほん]に住[す]み続[つづ]け{ていきます}。
mistakes.note: From now into the future is ていく.

skills.tip: Point at yourself or at today: towards = くる, away = いく.

skills.rule: るところ = about to, ているところ = right in the middle of, たところ = has just this moment, たばかり = only recently (as the speaker feels it).
skills.explain:
ところ means 'point'; the verb form before it picks the phase. Dictionary form: 今から出かけるところだ 'I'm just about to go out'. ている form: 今ご飯を作っているところだ 'I'm in the middle of cooking'. Past form: 今着いたところだ 'I've just this minute arrived'. This set answers 'what are you doing right now?' and suits the moment of a phone call or interruption.

たばかり also means 'just did', but measures time by feeling, not the clock: 先月結婚したばかり 'only got married last month' is fine, 先月結婚したところ is not. たばかり often explains a present situation (来たばかりで、まだ友達がいない) and can sit before a noun: 買ったばかりのパソコン.

So: seconds or minutes ago, use たところ (たばかり is also fine); days, months or longer, only たばかり.
patterns: [dictionary form] ところ  (about to)
[ている form] ところ  (in the middle of)
[た form] ところ  (has just)
[た form] ばかり  (only recently)

examples.jp: 今[いま]から{出[で]かけるところ}です。
examples.en: I'm just about to go out.

examples.jp: 今[いま]、晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を{作[つく]っているところ}です。
examples.en: I'm in the middle of making dinner right now.

examples.jp: たった今[いま]、駅[えき]に{着[つ]いたところ}です。
examples.en: I've just this moment arrived at the station.

examples.jp: 日本[にほん]に{来[き]たばかり}なので、まだ友達[ともだち]がいません。
examples.en: I've only just come to Japan, so I don't have any friends yet.

examples.jp: 先週[せんしゅう]{買[か]ったばかり}のパソコンが壊[こわ]れた。
examples.en: The computer I bought only last week broke.

contrast.note: 作っている is a plain 'am cooking'; 作っているところ zooms in on this exact moment, typically as an answer or excuse.
たところ is clock time, just now; たばかり is felt recency and can stretch to weeks or months.
Dictionary form is before the action; past form is after it. 食べるところ 'about to eat' vs 食べたところ 'just ate'.

mistakes.bad: 先月[せんげつ]{引[ひ]っ越[こ]したところ}です。
mistakes.good: 先月[せんげつ]{引[ひ]っ越[こ]したばかり}です。
mistakes.note: A month ago is not 'this moment'; felt recency needs たばかり.

mistakes.bad: 今[いま]から{食[た]べたところ}です。
mistakes.good: 今[いま]から{食[た]べるところ}です。
mistakes.note: 今から 'from now' means the action is still ahead: dictionary form.

skills.tip: Before, during, just after: る / ている / た + ところ; 'only recently' with any time word: たばかり.

skills.rule: Masu-stem + 始める starts, + 出す bursts into (a sudden, unplanned start), + 続ける keeps on, + 終わる finishes.
skills.explain:
These four attach to the masu-stem (食べ, 読み, 勉強し) and mark a phase of the action. 〜始める is a neutral start, deliberate or not: 日本語を勉強し始めた. 〜出す is a sudden, unexpected start, usually not under control: 赤ちゃんが泣き出した, 急に走り出した. Because it is sudden, 出す is not used in requests, invitations or plans: 'please start reading' is 読み始めてください.

〜続ける means 'keep on doing': 一日中降り続けた. 〜終わる means 'finish doing' and needs an action with a natural end, such as reading a book or eating a meal: 読み終わった. It does not fit weather or feelings; rain that stops is 雨がやむ. 〜終える is a more formal 'finish'.

All four conjugate like ordinary verbs: 始めます, 出した, 続けている, 終わったら.
patterns: [masu-stem] 始める  (start)
[masu-stem] 出す  (suddenly start)
[masu-stem] 続ける  (keep on)
[masu-stem] 終わる  (finish)

examples.jp: この本[ほん]はもう読[よ]み{終[お]わりました}。
examples.en: I've already finished reading this book.

examples.jp: 三年前[さんねんまえ]から日本語[にほんご]を勉強[べんきょう]し{始[はじ]めました}。
examples.en: I started studying Japanese three years ago.

examples.jp: 急[きゅう]に赤[あか]ちゃんが泣[な]き{出[だ]した}。
examples.en: The baby suddenly burst into tears.

examples.jp: 雨[あめ]が一日中[いちにちじゅう]降[ふ]り{続[つづ]けた}。
examples.en: It kept raining all day.

examples.jp: 姉[あね]は話[はな]し{始[はじ]める}と止[と]まらない。
examples.en: Once my older sister starts talking, she doesn't stop.

contrast.note: Both start; 出す adds 'suddenly, all at once' and cannot be requested or planned.

contrast.vs: 続ける vs ている
contrast.note: 降っている is 'is raining'; 降り続けている stresses that it has not stopped.

contrast.vs: 終わる vs てしまう
contrast.note: 読み終わる is neutral completion of the action; 読んでしまう adds 'all done' or regret.

mistakes.bad: では、教科書[きょうかしょ]を読[よ]み{出[だ]して}ください。
mistakes.good: では、教科書[きょうかしょ]を読[よ]み{始[はじ]めて}ください。
mistakes.note: 出す is a sudden, uncontrolled start; a request needs 始める.

mistakes.bad: やっと雨[あめ]が降[ふ]り{終[お]わりました}。
mistakes.good: やっと雨[あめ]が{やみました}。
mistakes.note: 終わる needs an action with a natural end; rain stops with やむ.

skills.tip: Start, burst, keep, finish: 始める, 出す, 続ける, 終わる on the masu-stem.
